mcqs.question: Why might a confident, well-delivered answer score lower on a behavioral rubric than an awkward one?
options: The rubric scores specific, evidence-backed competency anchors, and a confident answer with no concrete action or outcome gives the interviewer nothing to write down
Interviewers are trained to penalize confident candidates to reduce bias
Awkward answers are always more honest than polished ones
Confidence is not one of the competencies most companies score
mcqs.explanation: Scoring runs on named competencies backed by specific behavioral evidence, not on how the delivery felt — an answer with no concrete action or measurable outcome leaves the interviewer with nothing to anchor a rating to, regardless of how smooth it sounded.

mcqs.question: You're told your loop spreads behavioral competencies across every technical round instead of using one dedicated session. What does that imply for your prep?
options: You can skip behavioral prep since it's a minor add-on to technical rounds
Only the final round of the day will actually be scored behaviorally
You should prepare one long story and repeat it in every round for consistency
You stay switched on through the end of every round, since a 'technical' interviewer may score a competency in the last few minutes
mcqs.explanation: In the spread model, each interviewer typically owns one or two competencies tacked onto an otherwise technical session, so relaxing once the coding portion ends means missing signal you're still being scored on. Repeating one story everywhere risks looking rehearsed and doesn't map to different competencies.

mcqs.question: Two interviewers in the same loop independently note that your account of your role in a project changed between rounds. What effect does this typically have?
options: It only counts against you if you contradict yourself within the same round
It's a strong negative signal, often stronger than either individual round's score, because it undermines the story's factual reliability
None — interviewers don't compare notes until after an offer is extended
It only matters if the discrepancy is about the technical rounds, not behavioral ones
mcqs.explanation: Interviewers compare notes at debrief, and an independently-flagged inconsistency in a story's facts reads as unreliable evidence — which weighs more heavily than a single round's ordinary score, because it puts every other claim in the loop in question too.

mcqs.question: A candidate scores excellently on every coding round but gets a 'strong no' on ownership and collaboration. What commonly happens in the hire/no-hire debrief?
options: The technical score always wins since it's more objectively measured
The candidate is automatically re-routed to a different, less technical role
The strong-no on behavioral competencies can override strong technical scores, since teams treat it as a proxy for how the person will be to work with
The behavioral score is ignored unless the role is management
mcqs.explanation: Behavioral competencies are frequently treated as a proxy for day-to-day working relationships, which are hard to observe any other way pre-hire — so a strong-no there commonly overrides otherwise-strong technical performance rather than being outweighed by it.

mcqs.question: What is the practical consequence of treating a behavioral round as an informal chat that needs no preparation?
options: Interviewers automatically lower your score for being too casual
The round is rescheduled if the interviewer detects a lack of preparation
It has no real effect as long as the technical rounds go well
Vague, unrehearsed answers give the interviewer no concrete anchors to score, which tends to be recorded as 'no signal' and treated as risk rather than a pass
mcqs.explanation: A rubric with no concrete anchors to write down defaults to 'no signal,' and no signal reads as risk in a competitive loop — it is not a neutral outcome, and it isn't offset by strong technical rounds when behavioral is scored on its own terms.
